The Torah Teaching, Work and Leadership of the Amora Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
This survey sketches the portrait of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, one of the great Amoraim of the Land of Israel, examining his halakhic work, his thought and his pious conduct. The text emphasizes how he is historically distinguished from other sages with similar names, and details his unique contribution to the world of blessings and aggadah, based on a metaphysical conception of the order of creation and a recognition of the uniqueness of every particular in reality. Alongside learned give-and-take, the source describes a figure of an ascetic and a pious man (chasid) of spiritual power who subdues harmful forces, who is scrupulous about giving in secret and who merits constant heavenly providence. The closing section of the work is devoted to describing his sublime passing, accompanied by a dialogue with the Angel of Death and by the appearance of a pillar of fire attesting to his moral perfection and to his having fulfilled the entire Torah.

The Torah Teaching, Work and Leadership of the Amora Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
Introduction and Biography: The Historical Identity of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, who appears in the historical and Talmudic sources also under the names Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Chinena bar Pappa, or by the shortened forms Chananya and Chinena, was among the most prominent Amoraim of the Land of Israel of the third generation, active at the transition between the third and fourth centuries CE [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4]. His name, "Pappa," represents the Aramaic version of the common Greek name "Pappos," a fact reflecting the linguistic and cultural context in which he worked in the Land of Israel under Roman rule [cite: 3].
Rabbi Chanina belonged to the younger circle of the disciples of Rabbi Yochanan, although in the entire expanse of the Jerusalem Talmud he quotes his principal teacher directly only once, in tractate Bava Kamma [cite: 4, 5]. The bulk of his learning in the world of aggadah and derash he acquired from Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, whom he called by the title "Rabbi" and whose extraordinary esteem he won thanks to his exceptional mastery of the Holy Scriptures [cite: 3, 4]. In the framework of his halakhic and public activity his name is consistently linked with the great men of the generation in the Land of Israel, among them Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Zeira [cite: 1, 2, 3, 6]. He sat in judgment in the joint courts alongside Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and took an active part in shaping the legal and public rulings of the period [cite: 2, 7]. At the same time, he used to conduct frequent Torah discussions and disputes with his colleagues in the study hall, such as Rabbi Chama bar Chanina and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina, while his prominent disciples included Rabbi Il'a and Rav Ada bar Avimi [cite: 3, 5, 6].
Historical and Talmudic scholarship requires a scientific and careful distinction between Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa of the Land of Israel and other Talmudic figures with similar names, especially the Babylonian Amora Rav Pappa, who was active in the fifth generation in Babylonia and was a disciple of Abaye and Rava [cite: 8, 9, 10, 11]. This distinction is essential to prevent anachronism, since the Babylonian Rav Pappa was known as a wealthy businessman and a producer of date beer, and even had ten sons, one of whom was indeed called Chanina bar Pappa, but lived more than fifty years after the death of the Amora of the Land of Israel who is the subject of this study [cite: 8, 9, 10].
His Halakhic Teaching: Hermeneutics, Blessings and Derekh Eretz
Although the main fame of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa in Talmudic literature rests on his wondrous homilies in aggadah, he also left an indelible mark in the realms of halakha and practical hermeneutics [cite: 2, 3]. His halakhic approach was characterized by a phenomenological analysis of the details of the commandments and by an attempt to anchor the religious obligations of the individual within an overall system of social and cosmic responsibility.
A fundamental issue in which his interpretive conception finds expression is his defense of the view of Rabbi Yehuda regarding blessings over enjoyment and blessings over commandments, as cited in tractate Berakhot and tractate Sukkah [cite: 13]. Rabbi Yehuda held that general formulas of blessing do not suffice, but that one must assign a specific blessing to each and every species by itself, such as saying "Who creates the kinds of herbs" over the grasses of the field, or bless each and every commandment separately when many commandments lie before a person [cite: 13]. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa supported this approach and grounded it textually on the homily on the verse "Blessed be the Lord day by day," explaining that just as on each and every day one must give the Holy One, blessed be He, the blessings specific to that day, so too for each and every species and each and every commandment one must give the specific praise befitting it [cite: 13]. This conception reflects a religious outlook that sees supreme value in distinction and particularity, out of an understanding that every particular in creation and in the divine command represents a unique revelation of the divine will which must not be submerged and swallowed up in generality [cite: 13].
Out of a deep conceptual affinity with the importance of blessings over enjoyment, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa laid down a stringent ruling in tractate Berakhot, according to which anyone who derives benefit from this world without a blessing is as though he robs the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Congregation of Israel [cite: 3, 14]. His homily sharply links individual sin with its collective harm to the community, since according to the interpretation cited there, the sin of individuals who make light of giving thanks for food causes the agricultural produce in the Land of Israel to be stricken, and the entire public suffers a reduction of material abundance [cite: 14]. Thus the person who is lax about blessings becomes "the companion of a destroyer," and the Gemara likens him to Jeroboam son of Nebat, who sinned and caused Israel to sin [cite: 14].
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa applied his halakhic approach also to the inherent tension between Torah study and the labor of one's hands [cite: 14]. When he came to interpret the conceptual contradiction between the Torah's obligation of continuous study and the command "and you shall gather in your grain," he adopted the balanced view of Rabbi Yishmael [cite: 14]. According to his interpretation, the practice of derekh eretz and the combining of work are intended for completely righteous people who are not at the absolute spiritual level, for whom a practical combination of livelihood and study is required, whereas supremely righteous people who attain absolute spiritual fulfillment merit to have their work done by others [cite: 14].
In tractate Chullin, and also in the Ramban's work on the Talmud, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's halakhic interest in the question of grafting two kinds of herbs onto one another is documented [cite: 15]. This question reflects his attempt to apply the biblical prohibition of mixed seeds (kil'ei zera'im) to different kinds of grasses, out of his metaphysical conception that advocates preserving the original order of the work of creation and avoiding the mixing of the domains of life established by the Creator [cite: 15].
Further evidence of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's engagement with economic and messianic contexts appears in tractate Avodah Zarah, where a practical halakhic discussion is brought concerning the purchase of land in the Land of Israel after the destruction [cite: 16]. The baraita presents a chronological calculation according to which, if a person is offered a field worth a thousand dinars for the price of only one dinar, he should refrain from buying it if $400$ years have passed since the destruction of the Second Temple [cite: 16]. In the parallel calculation based on the count of years from the creation of the world, the baraita sets the turning point in the year $4231$ from creation, and the sages of the Gemara analyze the gap in years that results and put it at a difference of only $\Delta = 3$ years between the two historical systems of counting [cite: 16]. This discussion reveals the way in which Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa combined eschatological redemptive expectations with practical economic decisions about acquiring real estate in the Land of Israel under the yoke of foreign rule [cite: 16].
Theology and Aggadah: Cosmology, Divine Revelation and Historiosophy
The homiletic and aggadic teaching of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa presents a systematic and complex theology, which examines the tension between the changing divine revelation and the absolute unity of the Creator, and the role of the people of Israel vis-à-vis the nations of the world in the historical and metaphysical context.
A profound and original theological aspect appears in Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's homily on the modes of divine revelation to the people of Israel [cite: 17]. According to him, the Holy One, blessed be He, appeared before the people of Israel in a multiplicity of faces and emotional states:
"With an angry face, with an even face, with a friendly face, with a smiling face." [cite: 17]
To prevent the danger of a polytheistic conception or a dualistic corporealization because of the visual and emotional variety of these revelations, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa stressed that the Creator declared before the people that although they see Him in these changing forms and hues, He always remains one and unchanging being [cite: 17]. This homily offers a solution to the phenomenology of biblical anthropomorphism, and makes clear that the changes in religious emotion and in the experience of revelation are nothing but a reflection of the human vessels of reception, and not a change in the divine essence itself [cite: 17].
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explained the essential difference between the prophecy of Israel and the prophecy of the nations of the world by means of the parable of the king in his palace [cite: 3, 18]. Whereas the prophets of Israel merit direct revelation and complete speech, like a king who removes the curtains and speaks with his loved ones face to face, the prophets of the nations of the world, among them Balaam son of Beor, merit only partial and indirect revelation, likened to a king who speaks with strangers from behind a partition or curtain [cite: 3, 18].
In tractate Sanhedrin the homiletic power of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa finds expression in his analysis of the biblical history of the Kingdom of Judah and the subjugation of the people of Israel [cite: 19]. In his homily on the verse "Therefore shall you give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; the houses of Achzib shall be a deception to the kings of Israel," he describes how a heavenly voice (bat kol) went forth and flung at the sages of the generation and at the people their ingratitude toward the dynasty of King David [cite: 19]. The heavenly voice asked in rebuke:
"He who killed the Philistine and gave you Gath as an inheritance—will you give parting gifts to his sons?" [cite: 19]
This homily illustrates Rabbi Chanina's historiosophical conception, according to which national troubles and political destruction are bound up intrinsically with the moral and religious disregard of the spiritual heritage of the House of David [cite: 19]. A further interpretive dispute that highlights his historical sensitivity revolves around the figure of the biblical king Abijah son of Jeroboam, in which Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa disagreed with Rabbi Zeira in analyzing the good deeds and historical merits of the king that brought about his deliverance [cite: 3].
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's cosmological conception finds distinct expression in his famous homily on the song of creation and the conduct of the laws of nature, in which he described how the Prince of the World broke into song on hearing of the conduct of the grasses in the work of creation [cite: 1]. When the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded the trees to come forth "according to their kind," the grasses reasoned a fortiori (kal va-chomer) about themselves and understood that if the Creator does not desire mixture and chaos among the trees, all the more so is this required of them [cite: 1]. As they came forth distinct, each according to its kind, the Prince of the World recognized the beauty of the natural order and sang the verse "May the glory of the Lord endure forever; may the Lord rejoice in His works" [cite: 1]. The homily emphasizes the conception that nature itself is endowed with an inner understanding and a will to uphold the laws of morality and the metaphysical distinction established by the Creator [cite: 1].
Pious Conduct, Asceticism and the Subduing of Harmful Forces
The figure of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa is shaped in the Talmudic tradition as a symbol of supreme holiness, ascetic withdrawal and absolute commitment to a moral conduct that goes beyond the letter of the law [cite: 2, 3, 4, 6]. His deeds are described as having given him metaphysical mastery over the forces of nature and even over the world of demons and spirits [cite: 2, 3, 7, 20].
One of the strongest testimonies to his moral holiness is the story of his resistance to the temptations of an influential Roman matron [cite: 2, 3, 6]. To save himself from sin without harming the woman's dignity or arousing her political wrath, Rabbi Chanina offered a prayer or uttered a mystical formula that caused his whole body to be covered with boils, pustules and severe sores that made his appearance repulsive [cite: 2, 3, 6]. After the woman removed the sores by means of acts of sorcery, Rabbi Chanina was forced to flee and hide for the night in an abandoned bathhouse haunted by demons and harmful spirits [cite: 2, 3, 6]. His choice of this dangerous place stemmed from the clear knowledge that the woman would not dare to pursue him there, and by virtue of his deep piety he was saved from physical harm by the harmful spirits that ruled the place [cite: 3, 6].
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's public conduct included the secret distribution of charity to the poor in the dead of night, as a practical and scrupulous application of the words of Scripture "A gift in secret pacifies anger" [cite: 2, 3, 7, 20]. Since in the mystical tradition the night is considered the time of the exclusive dominion of the harmful forces, his nocturnal activity aroused opposition on the part of the prince of the spirits [cite: 2, 20]. One night the chief of the harmful spirits met him and flung at him the accusation of transgressing the world order:
"Did you not teach us thus, Rabbi: 'You shall not remove your neighbor's landmark'? Surely the night is the boundary allotted to the spirits and demons, so why do you enter our domain and distribute charity?" [cite: 2, 3, 20]
Rabbi Chanina was not deterred and answered him at once from Scripture, that the protective power of secret charity ("a gift in secret") stands above the natural laws of the harmful spirits and subdues their fury, and following his answer the prince of the spirits was forced to retreat and depart from the road [cite: 2, 3, 7]. This story demonstrates the conception according to which the pure moral deed grants a person absolute protection against the forces of impurity and destruction [cite: 2, 3].
The individual providence that accompanied Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa prevented him from erring in halakhic rulings and in the performance of religious acts [cite: 2, 7]. When it happened that he inadvertently erred on a halakhic detail concerning the laws of mourning, he was granted a heavenly revelation in a dream at night in which the verse "and you rebelled against the word of the Lord" was said to him [cite: 2, 3, 7]. This revelation enabled him to correct his error immediately, and it was regarded by his colleagues as a sign and wonder that his Torah was always directed toward the pure divine truth [cite: 2, 7].
Old Age, the Passing and the Heavenly Pillar of Fire
The moments of the death and passing of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, described in detail in tractate Ketubot, constitute the climax of his pious life story and illustrate the metaphysical veneration felt for him both in the material world and in the spiritual world [cite: 1, 4, 7, 21].
Because of his immense spiritual level and his full mastery over his inclination, Rabbi Chanina is described in the literature of the Sages as one who was on terms of close friendship with the Angel of Death [cite: 1, 7, 21, 22]. Kabbalists and homilists explained this wondrous friendship as an allegory for Rabbi Chanina's having completely subdued the evil inclination (identified in mystical literature with Satan and the Angel of Death), until the inclination ceased to be an enemy fighting the person and became a force subject to his authority and his spiritual will [cite: 22]. When his time came to depart from the world, the Angel of Death was commanded from heaven to carry out all the wishes of the pious man [cite: 1, 21, 22].
Rabbi Chanina asked the Angel of Death to grant him a reprieve of thirty days so that he could review all his learning, out of a desire to arrive in the World to Come with all his Torah ordered and clear in his hand [cite: 1, 4, 7, 21]. The Angel of Death granted his request [cite: 1, 4, 7, 21]. When the thirty days had passed the angel returned, and Rabbi Chanina demanded that he show him his designated place in the Garden of Eden, and even that he hand over to him the angel's menacing knife along the way so as to spare himself fear [cite: 1, 3, 7]. The Angel of Death refused to hand over the knife, claiming that a similar act done by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had led to Rabbi Yehoshua taking the knife, leaping into the Garden of Eden and swearing not to return [cite: 1, 3, 7, 22]. The angel asked Rabbi Chanina whether he thought he stood at the moral level of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rabbi Chanina answered with absolute self-assurance:
"Bring a Torah scroll and show me anything written in it that I have not fulfilled!" [cite: 1, 7, 21]
To challenge Rabbi Chanina's claim, the Angel of Death asked him whether in his life he had acted like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who used to attach himself to and embrace those afflicted with the contagious and deadly disease "ba'alei ra'atan" in order to study Torah with them, trusting that the Torah would protect them [cite: 1, 21, 23]. To this question Rabbi Chanina was forced to answer in the negative, and he admitted that he had not reached this extreme level of self-sacrifice [cite: 1, 21].
Although he had not reached the level of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the matter of the ra'atan sufferers, the absolute holiness of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa was proven beyond all doubt at the moment of his passing [cite: 1, 4, 7, 21]. Upon his passing, a heavenly pillar of fire ("amuda de-nura") descended and separated his bier from the crowd of mourners and sages who had come to pay him their last respects [cite: 1, 4, 7, 21]. The tradition of the Sages holds that such a pillar of fire appears only once or twice in a generation, for unique individuals alone [cite: 7, 21]. Abaye explained this wondrous phenomenon by stating that the pillar of fire descended in order to testify before all that the deceased had fulfilled the entire Torah without exception [cite: 23].
Because of the barrier of fire, the sages could not approach the body in order to attend to its burial [cite: 1, 3]. Rabbi Alexandri approached the bier of the deceased and addressed him with three different requests that he remove the separating fire [cite: 1, 3]. His first appeal, "Do it for the honor of the Torah scholars," was of no avail [cite: 1, 3]. His second appeal, "Do it for the honor of your father," also remained unanswered [cite: 1]. Only when he addressed him with the third and deepest request of all:
"Do it for the honor of your Torah." [cite: 1, 3]
did the heavenly pillar of fire withdraw and depart from the place, and thus the sages of the generation were able to bury him with the honor befitting such a spiritual giant [cite: 1, 3]. This sublime event sealed the life story of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, and gave double force to his eternal standing as one of the shapers of the spiritual and moral path of the Jewry of the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 2, 3].
